title: The Marble, the Beach Ball, and Space
markdown:
Aboard the Stardust Wanderer — a ship that wasn’t quite as grand as it sounded, but cozy, and theirs — Captain Elowen kept the helm. Her eyes held the twinkles of distant galaxies, a smile etched by starlight, a calm way about her, perfect for cosmic currents. Beside her, poring over a whirring datapad, was Nia. Nia loved data. Numbers, charts, graphs more than most people loved their favourite biscuits. Goggles perched on her nose magnified already wide intelligent eyes as she jotted every measurement. Fluttering about, occasionally pecking a loose wire that always seemed to spark gently, was Bramble, a rook with feathers as dark and glossy as polished obsidian, whistling jaunty scatterbrained tunes.

They were bound for the Great Nebula Nursery, whispered about in cosmic lullabies, where new stars were born from clouds of gas and dust. “Captain,” Nia sighed, tapping the pad, “the distance is just too much. I have the numbers. 4.37 light-years, logged precisely. But I can’t feel them. How can something be so far that light, the fastest thing there is, takes over four years to reach us? Like imagining a single grain of sand on an endless beach.” She wished she could see the distance, not just count it.

Elowen chuckled, distant chimes on a breeze. “That’s the curious thing about space. Numbers are useful. Sometimes you need to see the shape of the emptiness between them. Feel the vastness, not only measure it.”

Bramble, preening a stubborn feather, suddenly squawked. “Look! A comet!” Through the viewport, a shimmering streak of ice and dust drifted past, a celestial snowflake in slow motion, trailing a faint luminous tail. As it receded he ruffled. “It looks so small now. And our ship — a tiny forgotten crumb. Even that big comet was a speck against those star-lights.”

Nia watched it shrink into inky blackness. The pad could tell trajectory, composition, velocity. It could not show how the dark ocean made even a comet feel small. “The distances aren’t just lines on a map. They’re actual space. So much of it. An ocean without a shore.”

Elowen nodded. “You have the data. Now you need the scale. A trick my old space-teacher taught me.”

She guided them to the main cabin, a comfortable space with plush seating and constellation charts on the walls. From a compartment she took a small shiny marble and placed it carefully on a polished wooden table. “This is our Sun. Bright and warm. The heart of our solar system.”

Nia nodded, eyes fixed on the marble. “Small, but powerful.”

“Now.” Elowen set a peppercorn a good stretch along the table. “This is Jupiter. Not a grapefruit. The Sun is a giant compared with even the giant planet. See the space between our Sun and Jupiter?” Nia leaned closer. It was more than she had expected, even for the biggest neighbour. Bramble hopped from marble to peppercorn, then back, wings giving a little flutter. “A big jump for a bird!”

She held up a pin. “And this — Neptune, if we keep this scale — is not a beach ball. A pinhead. And it would not sit at the far end of this cabin. It would belong outside, down the corridor, still going.” The emptiness between the marble and the idea of that pin was the lesson. “That’s just our solar system, Nia. The planets are tiny. The gaps are not.”

Nia’s eyes widened behind her goggles. She looked around the cabin, imagining stretching the space until the pin vanished into the corridor. “Outside?”

“Yes,” said Elowen, eyes twinkling. “And if the Sun stays a marble, the next star — Proxima Centauri, the one in your 4.37 light-years — is not another cabin away. You could walk all day, and the next day, and you still would not have placed it. The numbers on your pad are not wrong. They are simply too large for a room.”

Nia looked from marble to peppercorn to the tiny pin, then out at the endless blackness peppered with lights. She pictured Bramble trying to fly from one to the other and getting lost in the immensity. The datapad’s figures felt less like cold facts and more like whispers lost in an enormous silent room.

“Oh.” Genuine wonder, deeper than any calculation. “It’s not just empty. It’s spacious. Incredibly, beautifully spacious.”

Elowen smiled. “That enormous space is part of why worlds have room to move. Orbits have room. New systems can form without crowding like marbles in a fist. It’s the canvas. The nebula we’re visiting paints on it.”

Nia finally understood. The vast distances were not only a problem to be solved with data. They were a wonder, a fundamental part of the universe’s grandeur. Scale. That was why the numbers had felt like sand. They were immense. She could not wait to see what other scales the universe held, beyond each vast distance — truths hidden in plain sight, waiting to be discovered.
characters: Nia (a data-loving explorer), Bramble (a rook), Elowen (a captain)
